<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin=par110 /><section begin=par110 />the four forms of the ''2nd fem. plur. imperative'' in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=32|verse=11}}, erroneously explained here in former editions, see now {{GHGpar|48|i}}). In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Na|chapter=3|verse=15}} the interchange of masc. and fem. serves to express totality (the nation in all its aspects). Cf., moreover, {{GHGpar|145|p}} on other noticeable attempts to substitute the corresponding masculine forms for the feminine.<section end=par110 />

<section begin=par111 />{{GHGpar-heading|111|The Imperfect with Wāw Consecutive}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|111|a}}
'''1.''' The {{GHGterm|imperfect}} with {{GHGterm|wāw consecutive}} ({{GHGpar|49|a}}–''g'') serves to express actions, events, or states, which are to be regarded as the temporal or logical sequel of actions, events, or states mentioned immediately<ref>On an apparent exception (the ''imperf. consec.'' at the beginning of whole books) see {{GHGpar|49|b}} note.</ref> before. The {{GHGterm|imperfect consecutive}} is used in this way most frequently as the ''narrative tense'', corresponding to the Greek ''aorist'' or the Latin ''historic perfect''. As a rule the narrative is introduced by a perfect, and then continued by means of imperfects with {{GHGterm|wāw consecutive}} (on this interchange of tenses cf. {{GHGpar|49|a}}, and especially {{GHGpar|112|a}}), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=3|verse=1}} ''now the serpent was'' ({{GHGheb|text=הָיָה}}) ''more subtil... and he said'' ({{GHGheb|text=וַיֹּאמֶר}}) ''unto the woman;'' {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=1|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=6|verse=9 ff.|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=10|verse=9 f.|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=15|verse=19|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=11|verse=12 ff. 27 ff.|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=14|verse=5 f.|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=15|verse=1 f.|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=16|verse=1 f.|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=21|verse=1 ff.|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=1 f.|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=25|verse=19 ff.|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=36|verse=2 ff.|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=37|verse=2|hidebook=1}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|111|b}}
Rem. 1. To this class belong some of the numerous ''imperfects consec.'' after various expressions of time, whenever such expressions are equivalent in meaning to a perfect<ref>Cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=45|verse=4}}, where the ''imperf. consec.'' is joined to an abrupt statement of the cause, and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=36|verse=7}}, where it is joined to an abrupt statement of the place.</ref> (viz. {{GHGheb|text=הָיָה|translate=it came to pass}}), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=6|verse=1}} ''in the year that king Uzziah died, I saw'' ({{GHGheb|text=וָֽאֶרְאֶה}}), &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=22|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=34|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=11|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=4|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=17|verse=57|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=21|verse=6|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=11|verse=1}}; on the use of {{GHGheb|text=וַיְהִי}} to connect expressions of time, see below, ''g''.—It is only in late books or passages that we find the simple {{GHGterm|perfect}} in a clause following an expression of time, as {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=17|verse=55}} (cf. Driver on the passage), {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=12|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=15|verse=8|hidebook=1}}, &c., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=10|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=15|verse=19|hidebook=1}}; the {{GHGterm|Perfect}} after {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} and the subject, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=7|verse=1}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|111|c}}
2. The continuation of the narrative by means of the imperfect consec. may result in a series of any number of such imperfects, e.g. there are forty-nine in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn.|chapter=1}}. As soon, however, as the connecting {{GHGterm|Wāw}} becomes separated from the verb to which it belongs, by the insertion of any word, the perfect necessarily takes the place of the imperfect, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=5}} ''and God called'' ({{GHGheb|text=וַיִּקְרָא}}) ''the light Day, and the darkness he called'' ({{GHGheb|text=וְלַח֫שֶׁךְ קָרָא}}) ''Night''; verse 10, 2:20, 11:3 and frequently.

{{GHGmargin-letter|111|d}}
3. Of two co-ordinate ''imperfects consecutive'' the former (as equivalent to a temporal clause) is most frequently subordinate in sense to the latter, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=28|verse=8 f.}} {{GHGheb|text=וַיַּרְא עֵשָׂו... וַיֵּ֫לֶךְ|translate=when Esau saw that..., he went}}, &c.; so also, frequently {{GHGheb|text=וַיִּשְׁמַע}}, &c., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=37|verse=21}}, &c. On the other hand, a second {{GHGterm|imperfect consecutive}} is seldom used in an explanatory sense, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=2|verse=10}} ({{GHGheb|text=וַתֹּ֫אמֶר|translate=for she said}}); cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=7|verse=12}}. Other examples of the imperfect consecutive, which apparently represent a progress in the narrative, in reality only refer to the same time, or explain what precedes, see {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=25}} ({{GHGheb|text=וַיִּֽהְיוּ|translate=they were}}; but {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=4|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=8|verse=8}} ''they are''); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=36|verse=14}} ({{GHGheb|text=וַתֵּ֫לֶד}}), 36:32 ({{GHGheb|text=וַיִּמְלֹךְ}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=1|verse=44}}.<section end=par111 /><noinclude>
